title: The 14-Year-Old Who Built a Working Nuclear Fusion Reactor
sources: Tom Clynes 'The Boy Who Played With Fusion' (2015) - In 2008, 14-year-old Taylor Wilson achieved nuclear fusion in his parents' garage in Reno, Nevada.
Intel International Science and Engineering Fair Archives - Wilson became the youngest person to build a working Farnsworth-Hirsch fusor, winning the Intel Young Scientist Award.

lines.text: At age fourteen, while other teenagers played video games, Taylor Wilson built a nuclear fusion reactor -
lines.caps: At 14, | while others played games, | Taylor Wilson | built a nuclear fusion reactor -

lines.text: Taylor was not an ordinary kid. By age ten, he had memorized the periodic table.
By age eleven, he was making homemade rocket fuel in his backyard.
Then he decided to master the ultimate secret of physics: harnessing the power of the sun.
He scoured the internet for vacuum chambers, deuterium gas, and a hundred-thousand-volt transformer.
Working alone in his garage workshop, he constructed a Farnsworth-Hirsch fusor.
Inside a steel sphere, high-voltage fields accelerated deuterium ions at hundreds of millions of degrees,
smashing atomic nuclei together until they fused into helium and released a blast of neutrons!
When radiation safety inspectors brought geiger counters into the house, needles spiked into the red.
Taylor had officially become the youngest human in history to achieve nuclear fusion.
He won the world's top science fairs and was personally invited to the White House to demonstrate nuclear detection to the President!
